title: BGP hijack infecting networks caused by a comedy of errors that’s not funny at all
gist: Attackers executed a BGP hijack of Softaculous IP space hosted at Hetzner Online, using a forged AS path and an over-permissive RPKI max-length setting to stay RPKI-valid, then obtained Let's Encrypt certificates and pushed malware disguised as Virtualizor updates to hosting providers and data centers. Softaculous admits its update clients did not cryptographically verify packages, and the hijack pulsed on and off across a 33-hour window before anyone reacted.

themes.theme: Anatomy of the supply chain attack

insights.claim: Attackers hijacked the IP space hosting Softaculous's software-update endpoint and its client and billing site, then used those addresses to push malware masquerading as updates to Virtualizor, a management platform for virtualized environments used by hosting providers and data centers.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-management software is a high-leverage supply chain target: one compromised update reaches hosting providers and data centers rather than end users.
insights.locator: Hackers carried out a supply chain attack

insights.claim: The malicious prefix 162.55.80.0/24 entered the global routing table a few minutes before 9 PM UTC on Friday along the path AS6204 (Zet.net), AS62390 (Nexon Host), and AS24940 (Hetzner Online), with BGP analyst Doug Madory assessing that the announcement likely originated with NexonHost through a compromise of its infrastructure or a customer exploiting security gaps.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The weakest link was a small downstream transit provider, not the large host — third-party AS hygiene is an underpriced risk for anyone dependent on a hosting supply chain.

insights.claim: The hijack ran intermittently over a 33-hour window: Hetzner Online reclaimed the address space 12 hours after it started by announcing the correct path, then stopped announcing it, letting the attacker repeat the hijack with almost 10 hours of Hetzner inaction the second time.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Detection and remediation latency measured in half-days is the real exposure metric; automated route monitoring is the cheap control that was missing.

insights.claim: Softaculous, Hetzner Online and downstream transit peer Zet.net all failed to properly monitor their systems and did not catch the hijacking until it had been running on and off for 22 hours.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Three independent parties each had the telemetry to catch this and none did — monitoring gaps compound rather than provide redundancy.
insights.locator: Like Hetzner Online, both Softaculous and Zet.net

insights.claim: Hetzner Online configured its RPKI Route Origin Authorization to allow prefix lengths anywhere between /24 and /16, so the attacker's more-specific /24 announcement was accepted as valid rather than filtered out.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A single permissive max-length parameter neutralizes RPKI protection entirely; auditing ROA max-length settings is a concrete, checkable control for any network operator.
insights.quote: Hetzner allowed more precise IP ranges (/24 when it should have been /16) to be announced, allowing the hijacker to impersonate them and automatically win on routing decisions.
insights.locator: Hetzner Online configured a parameter in RPKI

insights.claim: The attacker appended AS24940 as the rightmost ASN in the AS path, forging the origin so the route satisfied the ROA's origin requirement and was therefore treated as RPKI-valid and not dropped by networks that reject RPKI-invalid routes.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: RPKI ROV validates origin claims, not path authenticity — a structural limitation that path validation (ASPA/BGPsec) would be needed to close.
insights.locator: The hijack also included an AS path with a forged origin.

insights.claim: Because no existing route for 162.55.80.0/24 competed against it and routers prefer longest-prefix-match, all traffic destined for that range preferred the hijacked route over the legitimate 162.55.0.0/16 announcement.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Longest-prefix-match makes more-specific hijacks automatically win globally; defenders should pre-announce their own /24s to deny attackers that space.
insights.quote: because it was a more-specific route, any traffic destined for this IP range would prefer it over the legitimate route (162.55.0.0/16) due to routers’ preference for longest-prefix-match
insights.locator: Because there was no existing route

insights.claim: Because the /24 hijack spread globally, Let's Encrypt's geographically dispersed validation perspectives all reached the attacker's server instead of the legitimate domain operator, letting the attacker obtain valid TLS certificates despite the multi-vantage-point quorum requirement.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Multi-perspective domain validation fails against a globally propagated route hijack — a systemic weakness in the free-certificate issuance model.
insights.quote: causing the validation perspectives (and all other traffic) to reach the attacker’s server instead of the legitimate domain operator

insights.claim: Let's Encrypt says Certification Authority Authorization account binding, which limits acceptable issuers and validation methods, would have made the attack significantly more difficult.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: CAA account binding is an available, unused mitigation — a concrete hardening step for any organization whose domains gate software updates.
insights.locator: It also said that Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) account binding

insights.claim: Softaculous admitted its product update clients did not cryptographically verify update packages, so a modified package would not have been rejected, and the company cannot produce a definitive list of affected servers and is telling customers to treat every Virtualizor server as in scope.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Missing code signing turned a routing incident into a malware distribution event; unsigned update channels are a first-order due-diligence question for any software vendor.
insights.quote: Our product update clients did not yet cryptographically verify update packages, so a modified package would not have been rejected on that basis.

insights.claim: BGP hijacking has only rarely been used to spread malware, with prior known cases limited to the 2015 Hacking Team operation against a contracted target and a 2022 hijack of Amazon IP addresses used to host a smart contract that drained about $235,000 in bitcoin from users visiting the Celer Bridge cryptocurrency exchange.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Routing-layer attacks have historically monetized through crypto theft; their extension into software supply chains raises the damage ceiling considerably.
insights.locator: The incident is one of the few times

insights.claim: BGP hijackings are becoming less common thanks to widespread RPKI adoption, but this event shows it takes only one misconfiguration for those protections to fail.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Aggregate risk is falling while tail risk stays fat — security spend should target configuration auditing rather than further protocol adoption.
insights.quote: This weekend’s event demonstrates that it only takes one mistake for these protections to go off the rails.
insights.locator: Thankfully, BGP hijackings are becoming less common

insights.claim: BGP expert Ben Cartwright-Cox, creator of the BGP Tools suite, characterized the operators' lapses as "silly, preventable mistakes," and Softaculous, Hetzner and Zet.net did not immediately respond to emailed questions.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Expert consensus that the failure was elementary raises the odds of customer churn and liability exposure for the providers involved.
